docs.title: Lab Material: Introduction to Pthreads in C++
Objective
docs.text: This lab introduces you to the Pthreads (POSIX Threads) library in C++, emphasizing thread creation and the advantages of parallelism. By the end, you’ll be able to create threads, pass arguments to them, and understand how parallelism can enhance performance through a practical example.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Basic understanding of C++ (functions, pointers, etc.).
  • Familiarity with compiling and running C++ programs in a Unix-like environment (e.g., Linux).
  • A multi-core system to observe parallelism benefits.

docs.title: What is a Thread?
docs.text: A thread is a unit of execution within a program that runs concurrently with other threads. Unlike separate processes, threads share the same memory space, enabling efficient communication but requiring careful management to avoid conflicts.

docs.title: Why Use Threads?
docs.text: Threads enable multiple tasks to run simultaneously, leveraging multi-core processors to improve performance. For instance, a game might use one thread for graphics and another for physics calculations.

docs.title: Creating a Thread with Pthreads
docs.text: The pthread_create function is used to spawn a new thread. For simplicity, we’ll use default attributes (passing nullptr as the second argument). Here’s a step-by-step guide:

docs.title: Step-by-Step Example
docs.text:
1. Include Headers: Use <pthread.h> for Pthreads and <iostream> for output.
  2. Define a Thread Function: It must return void* and take a void* argument.
  3. Create the Thread: Call pthread_create with a thread identifier, attributes, function, and argument.
  4. Wait for Completion: Use pthread_join to wait for the thread to finish.

docs.title: Example Code
docs.text:
#include <pthread.h>
#include <iostream>

void* say_hello(void* arg) {
    std::cout << "Hello from the thread!\n";
    return nullptr;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t thread_id;
    pthread_create(&thread_id, nullptr, say_hello, nullptr); // Default attributes
    pthread_join(thread_id, nullptr); // Wait for thread to finish
    std::cout << "Main thread finished.\n";
    return 0;
}

./hello

docs.title: Passing Arguments to a Thread
docs.text: Threads often need data to perform tasks. Since pthread_create accepts a void* argument, you can pass any data type by casting it.

#include <pthread.h>
#include <iostream>

void* print_number(void* arg) {
    int* number = static_cast<int*>(arg);
    std::cout << "Thread received: " << *number << "\n";
    return nullptr;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t thread_id;
    int value = 100;
    pthread_create(&thread_id, nullptr, print_number, &value);
    pthread_join(thread_id, nullptr);
    std::cout << "Main thread done.\n";
    return 0;
}

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: To showcase parallelism’s benefits, we’ll compute prime numbers in a range—first sequentially, then in parallel—and compare their performance.

docs.title: Step 1: Define a CPU-Intensive Function (isPrime)
docs.text: We’ll check if a number is prime (only divisible by 1 and itself).

docs.title: Algorithm
docs.text:
1. If the number < 2, return false.
  2. For each integer i from 2 to √(number):
  3. If number % i == 0, return false.
  4. Return true if no divisors are found.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
#include <cmath>

bool isPrime(int num) {
    if (num < 2) return false;
    for (int i = 2; i <= std::sqrt(num); ++i) {
        if (num % i == 0) return false;
    }
    return true;
}

docs.title: Step 2: Sequential Prime Checking
docs.text: A single thread checks all numbers in a range.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
#include <vector>
#include <chrono>

void sequentialPrimeCheck(int start, int end, std::vector<bool>& results) {
    auto start_time = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    for (int i = start; i < end; ++i) {
        results[i - start] = isPrime(i);
    }
    auto end_time = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    std::chrono::duration<double> elapsed = end_time - start_time;
    std::cout << "Sequential time: " << elapsed.count() << " seconds\n";
}

docs.title: Step 3: Parallel Prime Checking
docs.text: Multiple threads divide the range, each processing a chunk.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
#include <pthread.h>
#include <vector>

struct ThreadData {
    int start, end;
    std::vector<bool>* results;
};

void* parallelPrimeCheck(void* arg) {
    ThreadData* data = static_cast<ThreadData*>(arg);
    for (int i = data->start; i < data->end; ++i) {
        (*data->results)[i - data->start] = isPrime(i);
    }
    return nullptr;
}

void runParallel(int num_threads, int start, int end, std::vector<bool>& results) {
    auto start_time = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    std::vector<pthread_t> threads(num_threads);
    std::vector<ThreadData> thread_data(num_threads);
    int chunk_size = (end - start) / num_threads;

    for (int i = 0; i < num_threads; ++i) {
        thread_data[i].start = start + i * chunk_size;
        thread_data[i].end = (i == num_threads - 1) ? end : start + (i + 1) * chunk_size;
        thread_data[i].results = &results;
        pthread_create(&threads[i], nullptr, parallelPrimeCheck, &thread_data[i]);
    }
    for (auto& thread : threads) {
        pthread_join(thread, nullptr);
    }
    auto end_time = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    std::chrono::duration<double> elapsed = end_time - start_time;
    std::cout << "Parallel time (" << num_threads << " threads): " << elapsed.count() << " seconds\n";
}

void runParallel(int num_threads, int start, int end, std::vector<bool>& results) {
    auto start_time = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();

int main() {
    const int START = 0;
    const int END = 100000; // Range: 0 to 99999
    const int NUM_THREADS = 4; // Adjust based on your CPU cores

docs.title: What is a Thread?
docs.text:
A thread is the smallest unit of execution within a process. A single process can have multiple threads running concurrently, all sharing the same memory space. This means they share global variables, the heap, and file descriptors. However, each thread has its own private program counter, stack, and set of registers. This shared memory model makes communication between threads easy but also introduces challenges that we will address later.

The main thread of your program starts when main() is called. This main thread can then create other threads, which we'll call child threads. This process is often referred to as forking.

docs.title: Why Use Threads?
docs.text:
• Parallelism: Execute multiple tasks simultaneously
  • Responsiveness: Keep applications responsive while performing background tasks
  • Resource sharing: Efficient communication between concurrent tasks
  • Performance: Better utilization of multi-core processors

docs.title: Thread Forking and Joining
docs.text:
The lifecycle of a thread involves creating it (forking) and then potentially waiting for it to finish (joining).

  • Forking: The pthread_create function creates a new thread and makes it executable. The operating system's scheduler will then decide when to run it. After the call, both the original (main) thread and the new (forked) thread are running concurrently.

  • Joining: A thread can wait for another thread to complete its execution by calling pthread_join. This is a blocking call. The thread that calls pthread_join will pause its execution until the target thread terminates. This is essential for ensuring that results computed by a child thread are available to the parent thread before the program exits.

docs.title: Creating a Thread with Pthreads
docs.text: The pthread_create function is used to fork a new thread. For simplicity, we’ll use default attributes (passing nullptr as the second argument). Here’s a step-by-step guide:

docs.title: Step-by-Step Example
docs.text:
1. Include Headers: Use <pthread.h> for Pthreads and <iostream> for output.
  2. Define a Thread Function: It must return void * and take a void * argument.
  3. Create the Thread (Fork): Call pthread_create with a thread identifier, attributes, function, and argument.
  4. Wait for Completion(Join): Use pthread_join to wait for the thread to finish.

docs.title: Example Code
docs.text:
#include <pthread.h>
#include <iostream>

void* say_hello(void* arg) {
    std::cout << "Hello from the thread!\n";
    return nullptr;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t thread_id;

    int result = pthread_create(&thread_id, nullptr, say_hello, nullptr); // Default attributes
    if (result != 0) {
        std::cerr << "Error creating thread!" << std::endl;
        return 1;
    }

    pthread_join(thread_id, nullptr); // Wait for thread to finish
    std::cout << "Main thread finished.\n";
    return 0;
}
Explanation:

  • #include <pthread.h>: This line includes the necessary header file for Pthread functions.
  • pthread_t thread_id;: This declares a variable of type pthread_t, which is used to identify the thread.
  • pthread_create(&thread_id, nullptr, say_hello, nullptr);: This is the core function for creating a new thread.
    • The first argument is a pointer to the pthread_t variable where the ID of the new thread will be stored.
    • The second argument is used to specify thread attributes. We pass NULL to use the default attributes.
    • The third argument is a pointer to the function that the new thread will execute. This function must have a void * (*)(void *) signature.
    • The fourth argument is a pointer to the argument that will be passed to the thread function. In this case, we are not passing any arguments, so it is NULL.
  • pthread_join(thread_id, NULL);: This function makes the main thread wait for the newly created thread to terminate.

docs.title: 2. Passing Arguments to a Thread
docs.text: Threads often need data to perform tasks. Since pthread_create accepts a void * argument, you can pass any data type by casting it.

docs.title: Passing a Single Value
docs.text:
You can pass a single value to a thread by casting a pointer to void *.

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>

void* printMessage(void* msg) {
    // Cast the void* argument back to its original type
    char* message = (char*) msg;
    std::cout << message << std::endl;
    return nullptr;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t thread1, thread2;
    const char* message1 = "This is thread 1.";
    const char* message2 = "This is thread 2.";

    // Create threads and pass a string literal to each
    int result = pthread_create(&thread1, nullptr, printMessage, (void*) message1);
    if (result != 0) {
        std::cerr << "Error creating thread!" << std::endl;
        return 1;
    }

    result = pthread_create(&thread2, nullptr, printMessage, (void*) message2);
    if (result != 0) {
        std::cerr << "Error creating thread!" << std::endl;
        return 1;
    }

    // Wait for the threads to finish
    pthread_join(thread1, nullptr);
    pthread_join(thread2, nullptr);

    return 0;
}
Explanation:

  • We cast the const char* to void* when calling pthread_create.
  • Inside the printMessage function, we cast the void* argument back to char* to use it.

docs.title: Passing Multiple Values
docs.text:
To pass multiple values, you must bundle them into a struct and pass a pointer to an instance of that struct.

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <string>

// A struct to hold multiple arguments for our thread
struct ThreadArgs {
    int id;
    std::string message;
};

void* printArgs(void* arg) {
    // Cast the void* back to our struct type
    ThreadArgs* args = (ThreadArgs*) arg;

    std::cout << "Thread ID: " << args->id
              << ", Message: '" << args->message << "'" << std::endl;

    return nullptr;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t thread1;

    // IMPORTANT: Allocate the struct on the heap, not the stack,
    // to ensure it still exists when the new thread accesses it.
    ThreadArgs* args = new ThreadArgs();
    args->id = 101;
    args->message = "Passing multiple values is easy!";

    // Create the thread, passing a pointer to the struct
    int result = pthread_create(&thread1, nullptr, printArgs, (void*) args);
    if (result != 0) {
        std::cerr << "Error creating thread!" << std::endl;
        return 1;
    }

    pthread_join(thread1, nullptr);

    // Free the dynamically allocated memory to avoid leaks
    delete args;

    return 0;
}

docs.title: 3. The Power of Parallelism
docs.text: Now, let's explore why using multiple threads can significantly speed up our programs. We'll do this by writing a program to count prime numbers in a given range, first sequentially and then in parallel.

docs.title: Measuring Execution Time: Monotonic Clocks
docs.text:
To measure the performance of our sequential and parallel code, we need an accurate timer. For benchmarking, we should use a monotonic clock. A monotonic clock is a clock that can only move forward and is not affected by system time changes (like a user manually changing the time or daylight saving adjustments). This property ensures that the time duration we measure between two points is always positive and accurately reflects the elapsed time. In C++, std::chrono::steady_clock is guaranteed to be monotonic and is the best choice for measuring time intervals.

Here are the steps to compute the execution time:

  1. Include the header file chrono: 
    #include <chrono>
  2. Set the clock to monotonic clock: 
    using clock = std::chrono::steady_clock;
  3. Get the starting time-point before executing the task: 
    clock::time_point start = clock::now();
  4. Get the ending time-point after executing the task: 
    clock::time_point end = clock::now();
  5. Compute the time duration: 
    clock::duration execution_time = end - start;
  6. Print out the duration time in (seconds, milliseconds, microseconds, etc): 
    std::cout << "Execution time is "
        << std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>(execution_time).count() 
        << "ms." << std::endl;

docs.title: The isPrime() Function
docs.text:
We need a function that does a fair amount of work to properly see the benefits of parallelism. Checking for prime numbers is a good example of a CPU-intensive task.

// A simple function to check if a number is prime

bool isPrime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) return false;    // no prime less than 2
    if (n == 2) return true;    // 2 is the only prime that is even
    if (n % 2 == 0) return false; // All even numbers are not prime.

    // Check odd divisors up to sqrt(n)
    for (int i = 3; i * i <= n; i+=2) {
        if (n % i == 0) return false;
    }
    return true;
}

Algorithm Explanation:

  1. If the number n < 2, return false.
  2. If the number n is 2, return true.
  3. If the number n is an even number, return false
  4. For each odd integer i from 3 to \(\sqrt n\):
  5. If n % i == 0, return false.
  6. Return true if no divisors are found.

We only need to check up to the square root because if a number n has a divisor larger than its square root, it must also have a divisor smaller than it.

docs.title: Sequential Prime Counting
docs.text:
Let's establish our baseline with a sequential (single-threaded) implementation:

#include <iostream>
#include <chrono>

// isPrime() function from above

int countPrimesSequential(int start, int end) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = start; i <= end; i++) {
        if (isPrime(i)) {
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

int main() {
    const int START = 1;
    const int END = 5000000;

    std::cout << "Counting primes from " << START << " to " << END << " (sequential)" << std::endl;

    // Measure execution time
    auto start_time = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();

    int primeCount = countPrimesSequential(START, END);

    auto end_time = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    auto duration = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>(end_time - start_time);

    std::cout << "Found " << primeCount << " prime numbers" << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Sequential execution time: " << duration.count() << " milliseconds" << std::endl;

    return 0;
}

Counting primes from 1 to 5000000 (sequential)
Found 348513 prime numbers
Sequential execution time: 756 milliseconds

docs.title: Parallel Prime Counting
docs.text: Now, let's parallelize this task by dividing the range among multiple threads.

docs.title: countPrimesSequential() Analysis
docs.text:
Our sequential function processes numbers one by one in a single thread:

  • Input: Range of numbers (start to end)
  • Process: Check each number individually
  • Output: Count of prime numbers
  • Limitation: Uses only one CPU core

docs.title: countPrimesParallel() Components
docs.text:
To parallelize this, we need three key components:

Component 1: Thread Data Structure 

struct ThreadData {
    int start;        // Starting number for this thread
    int end;          // Ending number for this thread
    int count;        // Store the count of primes found
    int threadId;     // For identification and debugging
};

Component 2: Thread Function 

void* countPrimesThread(void* arg) {
    ThreadData* data = static_cast<ThreadData*>(arg);

    std::cout << "Thread " << data->threadId 
              << " processing range [" << data->start 
              << ", " << data->end << "]" << std::endl;

    data->count = 0;
    for (int i = data->start; i <= data->end; i++) {
        if (isPrime(i)) {
            data->count++;
        }
    }

    std::cout << "Thread " << data->threadId 
              << " found " << data->count << " primes" << std::endl;

    return nullptr;
}

Component 3: Work Distribution Strategy Let us do computation decompsition (data parallelism) according to the lecture: 

// Divide the work evenly among threads
int block_length = (END - START + 1) / NUM_THREADS;
for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; i++) {
    threadData[i].start = START + i * block_length;
    threadData[i].end = (i == NUM_THREADS - 1) ? END : threadData[i].start + block_length - 1;
    threadData[i].threadId = i;
}

Let assume that START = 0 and END = 999:

The diagram below visually shows how the range [0, 999] is partitioned into 4 equal segments (250 units each), with the last thread taking exactly 250 units in this case (since 1000 is divisible by 4). For uneven divisions (e.g., range 0-1000 with 4 threads), Thread 3 would get [750, 1000] (251 units).

docs.title: Key elements explained:
docs.text:
1. Initialization:

    • START = 0, END = 999, NUM_THREADS = 4
    • block_length = (999 - 0 + 1) / 4 = 250 (integer division)

  2. Work Distribution:

    • Thread 0: [0, 249] \(= (0 + 0×250)\) to \((0 + 0×250 + 250 - 1)\)
    • Thread 1: [250, 499] \(= (0 + 1×250)\) to \((0 + 1×250 + 250 - 1)\)
    • Thread 2: [500, 749] \(= (0 + 2×250)\) to \((0 + 2×250 + 250 - 1)\)
    • Thread 3: [750, 999] \(= (0 + 3×250)\) to END (special last thread case)

  3. Special Handling for Last Thread:

    • The last thread (Thread 3) gets the remaining range
    • Ensures all values from START to END are covered
    • Handles cases where the range isn't perfectly divisible by thread count

docs.title: How the Calculation Works:
docs.text:
int block_length = (END - START + 1) / NUM_THREADS;  // 1000/4 = 250

// Thread 0:
start = 0 + 0*250 = 0
end = 0 + 250 - 1 = 249

// Thread 1:
start = 0 + 1*250 = 250
end = 250 + 250 - 1 = 499

// Thread 2:
start = 0 + 2*250 = 500
end = 500 + 250 - 1 = 749

// Thread 3 (last thread):
start = 0 + 3*250 = 750
end = END = 999  // Instead of 750+250-1=999

This distribution ensures:

  • Equal workload for all threads (except possibly last thread)
  • Complete coverage from START to END
  • No overlapping ranges
  • Efficient division with O(1) calculation per thread
  • Handles remainder values automatically in last thread

docs.title: Full Program
docs.text:
#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <chrono>

struct ThreadData {
    int start;
    int end;
    int count;
    int threadId;
};

bool isPrime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) return false;
    if (n == 2) return true;
    if (n % 2 == 0) return false;

    for (int i = 3; i * i <= n; i += 2) {
        if (n % i == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

void* countPrimesThread(void* arg) {
    ThreadData* data = static_cast<ThreadData*>(arg);

    std::cout << "Thread " << data->threadId 
              << " processing range [" << data->start 
              << ", " << data->end << "]" << std::endl;

    data->count = 0;
    for (int i = data->start; i <= data->end; i++) {
        if (isPrime(i)) {
            data->count++;
        }
    }

    std::cout << "Thread " << data->threadId 
              << " found " << data->count << " primes" << std::endl;

    return nullptr;
}

int countPrimesParallel(int start, int end, int numThreads) {
    pthread_t* threads = new pthread_t[numThreads];
    ThreadData* threadData = new ThreadData[numThreads];

    // Distribute work among threads
    int block_length = (end - start + 1) / numThreads;

    std::cout << "Creating " << numThreads << " threads for parallel processing..." << std::endl;

    // Create threads
    for (int i = 0; i < numThreads; i++) {
        threadData[i].start = start + i * block_length;
        threadData[i].end = (i == numThreads - 1) ? end : threadData[i].start + block_length - 1;
        threadData[i].threadId = i;
        threadData[i].count = 0;

        int result = pthread_create(&threads[i], nullptr, countPrimesThread, &threadData[i]);
        if (result != 0) {
            std::cerr << "Error creating thread " << i << std::endl;
            return 1;
        }
    }

    // Wait for all threads to complete
    for (int i = 0; i < numThreads; i++) {
        pthread_join(threads[i], nullptr);
    }

    // Combine counts from all threads
    int totalPrimes = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < numThreads; i++) {
        totalPrimes += threadData[i].count;
    }

    delete[] threads;
    delete[] threadData;

    return totalPrimes;
}

// Sequential version for comparison
int countPrimesSequential(int start, int end) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = start; i <= end; i++) {
        if (isPrime(i)) {
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

int main() {
    const int START = 1;
    const int END = 100000;
    const int NUM_THREADS = 4;

    std::cout << "=== Prime Number Counting Performance Comparison ===" << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Range: " << START << " to " << END << std::endl << std::endl;

    // Sequential execution
    std::cout << "1. Sequential Execution:" << std::endl;
    auto start_time = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    int sequentialResult = countPrimesSequential(START, END);
    auto end_time = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    auto sequentialDuration = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>(end_time - start_time);

    std::cout << "Found " << sequentialResult << " prime numbers" << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Sequential time: " << sequentialDuration.count() << " ms" << std::endl << std::endl;

    // Parallel execution
    std::cout << "2. Parallel Execution (" << NUM_THREADS << " threads):" << std::endl;
    start_time = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    int parallelResult = countPrimesParallel(START, END, NUM_THREADS);
    end_time = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    auto parallelDuration = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>(end_time - start_time);

    std::cout << "Found " << parallelResult << " prime numbers" << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Parallel time: " << parallelDuration.count() << " ms" << std::endl << std::endl;

    // Performance analysis
    std::cout << "=== Performance Analysis ===" << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Correctness check: " << (sequentialResult == parallelResult ? "PASSED" : "FAILED") << std::endl;

    if (parallelDuration.count() > 0) {
        double speedup = static_cast<double>(sequentialDuration.count()) / parallelDuration.count();
        std::cout << "Speedup: " << speedup << "x" << std::endl;
        std::cout << "Efficiency: " << (speedup / NUM_THREADS) * 100 << "%" << std::endl;
    }

    return 0;
}

The program above will first count primes sequentially and then do it in parallel, finally printing a comparison of the results.

docs.title: Fibonacci Series
docs.text:
Let us assume the following fibonacci series:

\[ 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, \dots \]

This series can be defined mathematically as follows:

\[ fib(n) = \begin{cases} 1 & n \leq 1 \\ fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) & n > 1 \end{cases} \]

This implies that

  1. \(fib(0) = 1\)
  2. \(fib(1) = 1\)
  3. \(fib(2) = fib(1) + fib(0) = 1 + 1 = 2\)
  4. \(fib(3) = fib(2) + fib(1) = 2 + 1 = 3\)
  5. \(fib(4) = fib(3) + fib(2) = 3 + 2 = 5\)
  6. and so on.

Let us implement the fibonacci series using a recursive function:

unsigned long long fib (unsigned int n)
{
    if (n <= 1)
        return 1;
    else
        return fib(n-1) + fib(n-2);
}

The purpose of implementing fibonacci series recursively is that the running time is exponential. To see that, run the following program by clicking the button below:

#include <iostream>

using namespace std;

unsigned long long fib(unsigned int);

int main()
{
    cout << "fib(30) = " << fib(30) << endl;
    cout << "fib(40) = " << fib(40) << endl;
    cout << "fib(45) = " << fib(45) << endl;
    cout << "fib(48) = " << fib(48) << endl;

    return 0;
}

unsigned long long fib(unsigned int n)
{
    if (n <= 1)
        return 1;
    else
        return fib(n-1) + fib(n-2);
}
Jump to the code @ OnlineDBG

If you run the code, you should observe that fib(30) will be promptly printed out. fib(40) may take half second to be printed. fib(45) will take 5-6 seconds. But fib(48) will take significant amount of time; almost 26 seconds. All these estimations are based on the CPU speed of my PC.

docs.title: The Execution Time
docs.text:
The execution time is the time taken by the system to execute a task. We can compute the execution time using the std::chrono library introduced in C++ 11. Here are the steps to compute the execution time:

  1. Include the header file chrono: 

    #include <chrono>

  2. Set the clock to monotonic clock: 

    using clock = std::chrono::steady_clock;

  3. Get the starting time-point before executing the task: 

    clock::time_point start = clock::now();

  4. Get the ending time-point after executing the task: 

    clock::time_point end = clock::now();

  5. Compute the time duration: 

    clock::duration execution_time = end - start;

  6. Print out the duration time in (seconds, milliseconds, microseconds, etc): 

    std::cout << "Execution time is "
          << std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>(execution_time).count() 
          << "ms." << std::endl;

Here is the complete program: 

#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>

unsigned long long fib(unsigned int);

int main()
{
    using clock = std::chrono::steady_clock;
    clock::time_point start = clock::now();

    // we need to know the execution time taken by fib(45)   
    std::cout << "fib(45) = " << fib(45) << std::endl;

    clock::time_point end = clock::now();

    clock::duration execution_time = end - start;
    std::cout << "Execution time is " 
              << std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>(execution_time).count() 
              << "ms." << std::endl;
}

unsigned long long fib(unsigned int n)
{
    if (n <= 1)
        return 1;
    else
        return fib(n-1) + fib(n-2);
}

docs.title: Parallelize the Fibonacci series
docs.text:
In this lab, we are going to parallelize a serial program using POSIX pthread. To read more about POSIX pthread, visit LLNL High Performance Computing (HPC) or visit https://randu.org/tutorials/threads/.

To create a thread:

  1. You need to put the task in a function.

  2. The API to create a thread is pthread_create(). This function needs 4 arguments:

    1. When a thread is created, the API function returns (as argument) the thread handler (thread identifier). The data type of thread handler is pthread_t.
    2. Thread attributes to apply to the created thread. For the purpose of this course, you pass only NULL, which means the default attributes.
    3. The function/task to be executed by the created thread.
    4. The argument to be passed to the above function.

docs.title: STEP (1): Define your task as a function
docs.text:
We need to modify our serial program by defining a new function to compute the fibonacci series:

void computeFib()
{
    for (int n = 0; n < 48; n += 1)
        cout << "fib(" << n << ") = " << fib(n) << endl;
}
Now our goal is create multiple processors (threads) to execute the above function. However, each processor should execute a sub-domain out of the domain\([0, 48)\).

docs.title: STEP (2): Computation decomposition
docs.text:
Let us do computation decompsition according to the lecture (Listen to the lecture before proceeding):

void computeFib(int id)
{
    int block_length = N / NP; // divide N to NP processors
    int start = id * block_length;
    int end = start + block_length;

    for (int n = start; n < end; n += 1)
        cout << "fib(" << n << ") = " << fib(n) << endl;
}
where

  • N is a constant identifier that represents the value 48.
  • NP is a constant identifier that represents the number of processors.

Now, let us write the whole program serially, i.e., without creating processors (or threads): 

#include <iostream>

using namespace std;

unsigned long long fib(unsigned int);
void computeFib(int);

const int N = 16;   // data size
const int NP = 4;   // number of processors

int main()
{
    computeFib(0);  // this will be the task for P0
    computeFib(1);  // this will be the task for P1
    computeFib(2);  // this will be the task for P2
    computeFib(3);  // this will be the task for P3

    return 0;
}

void computeFib(int id)
{
    cout << "Processor (" << id << ") started ..." << endl;
    int block_length = N / NP; // divide N to NP processors
    int start = id * block_length;
    int end = start + block_length;

    for (int n = start; n < end; n += 1)
        cout << "fib(" << n << ") = " << fib(n) << endl;
    cout << "Processor (" << id << ") finished." << endl;
}

unsigned long long fib(unsigned int n)
{
    if (n <= 1)
        return 1;
    else
        return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
}

Remarks

  • Remember the above program is still a serial program. But it can easily be converted to parallel program by adding pthread_create().
  • The program will compute the fibonacci series from 0 up to 15
  • Run the program @ OnlineGDB. It should be executed very quickly.

  • We divided the range from 0 up to 15 into 4 jobs:

    1. Job 1: computeFib(0) (should be assigned to processor 0)
    2. Job 2: computeFib(1) (should be assigned to processor 1)
    3. Job 3: computeFib(2) (should be assigned to processor 2)
    4. Job 4: computeFib(3) (should be assigned to processor 3)

  • The argument in computeFib() should be the processor ID.

  • Observe the range of values to be computed for each processor/thread.

  • The details of the ranges is summarized in the following table:

    Processors Ranges P0 0 1 2 3 P1 4 5 6 7 P2 8 9 10 11 P3 12 13 14 15

    Processor P0 will compute the fibonacci of 0, 1, 2 and 3. Processor P1 will compute the fibonacci of 4, 5, 6 and 7, and so on.

docs.title: STEP (3): Create a thread for each job
docs.text:
Now, we need to run the four jobs in parallel using threads. In total, the program needs 4 threads. The main() function is modified as follows:

#include <pthread>
.
.
int main()
{
    pthread_t t0, t1, t2, t3;  // four threads

    // create a thread --> computeFib(0)
    pthread_create(&t0, NULL, computeFib, 0);

    // create a thread --> computeFib(1)
    pthread_create(&t1, NULL, computeFib, 1);

    // create a thread --> computeFib(2)
    pthread_create(&t2, NULL, computeFib, 2);

    // create a thread --> computeFib(3)
    pthread_create(&t3, NULL, computeFib, 3);

    // now wait for all threads to finish
    pthread_join(t0, NULL);
    pthread_join(t1, NULL);
    pthread_join(t2, NULL);
    pthread_join(t3, NULL);

    return 0;
}

C++ may emit an error message if you try to compile the above code. This is due to type mismatch. We fixed this issue in the next step.

docs.title: Data Parallism
docs.text:
In the previous lab, we have distributed the computation of Fibonacci series among 4 processors (threads). Each processor will compute \(n/np\) elements where \(n\) is the number of data elements and \(np\) is the number of processors.

Let us examine again our distribution when \(n = 48\) and \(np = 4\).

Processors Ranges P0 from 0 up to 11 P1 from 12 up to 23 P2 from 24 up to 35 P3 from 36 up to 47

Processor P0 will compute the Fibonacci of \(0, 1, 2, \dots, 11\). Processor P1 will compute the Fibonacci of \(12, 13, \dots, 23\), and so on.

Here is the parallel program that has been introduced in Lab (1):

Fib version (1)
#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>

using namespace std;

const int N = 48;   // data size
const int NP = 4;   // number of processors

unsigned long long fib (unsigned int);
void computeFib (int);

int main()
{
    pthread_t t0, t1, t2, t3;

    pthread_create(&t0, NULL, (void *(*)(void *))computeFib, (void *)0);
    pthread_create(&t1, NULL, (void *(*)(void *))computeFib, (void *)1);
    pthread_create(&t2, NULL, (void *(*)(void *))computeFib, (void *)2);
    pthread_create(&t3, NULL, (void *(*)(void *))computeFib, (void *)3);

    pthread_join(t0, NULL);
    pthread_join(t1, NULL);
    pthread_join(t2, NULL);
    pthread_join(t3, NULL);

    return 0;
}

void computeFib(int id)
{
    cout << "Processor (" << id << ") started ..." << endl;
    int block_length = N / NP; // divide N to NP processors
    int start = id * block_length;
    int end = start + block_length;

    for (int n = start; n < end; n += 1)
        cout << "fib(" << n << ") = " << fib(n) << endl;

    cout << "Processor (" << id << ") finished." << endl;
}

unsigned long long fib(unsigned int n)
{
    if (n <= 1)
        return 1;
    else
        return fib(n-1) + fib(n-2);
}

When I run the above program in my laptop, the running time will be approximately 40s. This is the same running time for the serial version. So, we did not benefit from the parallel hardware!

If you observe the output of the previous program, you will see that P0, P1, and P2 will finish quickly, while P3 is still running. This implies that the distribution is not fair among the processors. Notice that Processor P3 calculates fib(36), fib(37),..., fib(46) and fib(47). We know that the running time of fib() function is exponential and explodes when \(n>40\). Unfortunately, all data items greater than 40 are assigned to a single processor, which is P3.

docs.title: Changing the data distribution
docs.text:
We need to distribute the data such that the data items above 40 are distributed among the processors. One possible solution is illustrated in the following table (Data Partition Table) (where \(n = 16\)):

Processors Assignments P0 0 4 8 12 P1 1 5 9 13 P2 2 6 10 14 P3 3 7 11 15

The data items are distributed in round-robin fashion. P0 gets data item 0, P1 gets data item 1, P2 gets data item 2, P3 gets data item 3, P0 gets data item 4, and so on. This distribution is known as Cyclic Partition.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
Let us implement the cyclic distribution. We only need to modify computeFib() function.

void computeFib(int id)
{
    cout << "Processor (" << id << ") started ..." << endl;

    int start = id;
    int end = N - 1;

    for (int n = start; n <= end; n += NP)
        cout << "fib(" << n << ") = " << fib(n) << endl;

    cout << "Processor (" << id << ") finished." << endl;
}

docs.text: Assume we have a file that contains one million decimal numbers. We need to read these numbers and calculate their sum.

docs.title: The Serial Program
docs.text:
Let us write a SERIAL program to solve the above problem. 

/*
    This program reads N values from a text file. 
    Then, it calculates their sum.
*/
#include <iostream>
#include <fstream>
#include <iomanip>

using namespace std;

constexpr unsigned long N = 1'000'000;    // C++14

int main()
{
    ifstream dataFile;

    dataFile.open("mydata.txt");
    if (dataFile.fail())
    {
        cerr << "Cannot open mydata.txt file" << endl;
        return 1;
    }

    double sum = 0;
    double x;
    for (int i=0; i<N; i++) {
        dataFile >> x;
        sum = sum + x;
    }
    dataFile.close();

    printf("Sum = %.1f", sum);

    return 0;
}

The output is:

Output

Sum = 49965869.8

The above program assumes we know the number of values in the mydata.txt file. If we don't know, then we can update Lines 25-28 as follows:

    unsigned long N = 0;
    while (dataFile >> x) {
        sum = sum + x;
        N = N + 1;
    }

What is the expected sum?

The numbers in the file are generated using RAND()*100 in Excel program and repeated one million times. Click here to download the file [5MB].

We can estimate the sum of those values as follows. Let's consider n independent standard uniform random variables, denoted as \(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n\), each uniformly distributed on the interval \([0, 100]\). We want to estimate the expected value of their sum, which can be expressed as:

\[ E(X_1 + X_2 + \ldots + X_n) \]

The key property we'll use here is the linearity of expectation. It states that for any random variables \(Y_1, Y_2, \ldots, Y_n\), if their expectations exist, then:

\[ E(Y_1 + Y_2 + \ldots + Y_n) = E(Y_1) + E(Y_2) + \ldots + E(Y_n) \]

Applying this to our case, where \(Y_i = X_i\), we have:

\[ E(X_1 + X_2 + \ldots + X_n) = E(X_1) + E(X_2) + \ldots + E(X_n) \]

Since each \(X_i\) is uniformly distributed on \([0, 100]\), their expected value is:

\[ E(X_i) = \frac{100-0}{2}=50 \]

Therefore:

\[ E(X_1 + X_2 + \ldots + X_n) = n \cdot 50 = 50n \]

So, \(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i \approx 50n\). Hence, you can test the program several times with different values of N. In each run, you can estimate the expected sum.

docs.title: The Parallel Program
docs.text:
We are going to embarrasingly parallelize the serial program by dividing the work among NP threads/processes. In particular, we are going to parallelize the following code:

    double sum = 0;
    for (int i=0; i<N; i++) 
        sum = sum + x[i];

The data items in the array x will be distributed among the NP threads, as we did in Lab(2). All threads are going to execute a single task, named computeSum(), to emulate SPMD. Then, we manually assign an ID number for each thread, as depicted in the following diagram:

The computeSum() is implemented as follows:

void *computeSum (void *tid)
{
    int id = (int)(uintptr_t)tid;
    int block_length = N / NP;
    int start = id * block_length;
    int end = start + block_length;

    for (int i=start; i<end; i++) {
        sum = sum + x[i];
    }

    return nullptr;
}

void * data type

You may notice that the function computeSum() has the following prototype: 

    void *computeSum (void *);
This is the default prototype of the thread function as mentioned in POSIX standard. It means the thread function takes an object (any object) and returns an object (any object).

Since, we are passing an integer value, we must convert it from int to void * using type casting operator(s). Then, inside the thread function, we reverse the type casting (i.e., from void * to int).

docs.title: Thread Synchronization
docs.text:
The program in Exercise (1) has a serious BUG. All threads are accessing and modifying the shared variable sum. This problem is known as race condition, because the threads or processes are in a "race" to carry out the highlighted operation:

for (int i=start; i<end; i++)
    sum = sum + x[i];

Therefore, Line 69 is a critical section. Now, it's our job as programmers to ensure mutually exclusive access to the critical section by using mutex (or simply lock). To add a mutex:

  1. Declare a mutex variable (globally) as follows: 

    pthread_mutex_t mtx;

  2. Initialize the mutex (should be initialized before forking any thread): 

    pthread_mutex_init(&mtx, nullptr);

  3. Finally, protect the critical section by using the mutex: 

    for (int i=start; i<end; i++) {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&mtx);
    sum = sum + x[i];
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&mtx);
}

Here is the revised and complete lab tutorial.

docs.title: Lab Overview
docs.text: This lab provides a hands-on introduction to concurrent programming in C++ using the POSIX Threads (Pthreads) library. You'll learn the fundamental concepts of creating and managing threads to perform tasks in parallel. The tutorial will first guide you through thread creation and data passing. Then, you'll build a program that demonstrates the performance benefits of parallelism by comparing a sequential task to a multithreaded one. Finally, you'll learn about the critical problem of race conditions and how to solve it using mutexes for thread synchronization.

docs.title: Lab Objectives
docs.text:
Upon completing this lab, you will be able to:

  • ✅ Explain the lifecycle of a thread and how it differs from a process.
  • ✅ Write C++ code to create, manage, and join threads using the Pthread library.
  • ✅ Pass single or multiple arguments to a thread function.
  • ✅ Implement a parallel algorithm to speed up a computationally intensive task.
  • ✅ Measure and analyze the performance gains using metrics like speedup and efficiency.
  • ✅ Identify race conditions and protect shared data using mutexes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Basic C++ Knowledge: You should be comfortable with C++ syntax, functions, data types, pointers, and structs.
  • Development Environment: A Unix-like environment (Linux, macOS, or Windows Subsystem for Linux) with a C++ compiler (like g++) installed.
  • Command-Line Familiarity: Basic experience with compiling and running C++ programs from the terminal is necessary. To compile a Pthread program, you must link the pthread library using the -pthread flag: g++ your_program.cpp -o your_program -pthread.

docs.title: 1. Thread Creation
docs.text: In this section, you'll learn the basics of creating and managing a new thread of execution within your program.

docs.title: What is a Thread?
docs.text:
A thread is the smallest unit of execution within a process. A single process can have multiple threads running concurrently, all sharing the same memory space (like global variables and the heap). However, each thread has its own private program counter, stack, and set of registers. This shared memory model makes communication between threads efficient but also introduces synchronization challenges.

The main thread of your program starts when main() is called. This main thread can then create other threads. This process is often referred to as forking.

docs.title: Thread Forking and Joining
docs.text:
• Forking: The pthread_create function creates a new thread. After the call, the original (parent) thread and the new (child) thread run concurrently.

    Diagram: Thread Forking 

    graph TD
    A[Main Thread] --> B{pthread_create()};
    B --> C[Main Thread Continues];
    B --> D[New Thread Executes];

  • Joining: A thread can wait for another thread to complete by calling pthread_join. This is a blocking call, pausing the calling thread until the target thread terminates. This is essential for retrieving results computed by a child thread.

    Diagram: Thread Joining 

    graph TD
    subgraph Parallel Execution
        A[Main Thread]
        B[Child Thread]
    end
    A -- Runs Concurrently --> C{pthread_join(child)};
    B -- Runs Concurrently --> D[Finishes Task];
    D --> C;
    C -- Resumes Execution --> E[Main Thread Continues];

docs.title: Creating a Simple Thread
docs.text:
To get started, you must include the pthread.h header file. Let's create a thread that prints a simple message.

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>

// The function that the new thread will execute.
void* myFirstThread(void* arg) {
    std::cout << "Hello from the new thread!" << std::endl;
    return nullptr;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t thread_id; // Opaque variable to store the thread identifier

    std::cout << "Main thread: Creating a new thread." << std::endl;

    // Create the new thread
    pthread_create(&thread_id, nullptr, myFirstThread, nullptr);

    // Wait for the created thread to finish its execution
    pthread_join(thread_id, nullptr);

    std::cout << "Main thread: The new thread has finished." << std::endl;

    return 0;
}

Explanation:

  • #include <pthread.h>: Includes the Pthread library.
  • nullptr vs NULL: We use nullptr, the modern C++ standard for representing a null pointer, instead of the older C-style NULL macro.
  • pthread_create(&thread_id, nullptr, myFirstThread, nullptr): Creates the thread.
    • 1st argument: A pointer to thread_id to store the thread's identifier.
    • 2nd argument: A pointer to thread attributes; nullptr specifies default attributes.
    • 3rd argument: A pointer to the function the thread will execute.
    • 4th argument: A void* pointer to the argument for the thread function.
  • pthread_join(thread_id, nullptr): The main thread waits here until the thread identified by thread_id completes.

Sample Output:

Main thread: Creating a new thread.
Hello from the new thread!
Main thread: The new thread has finished.

docs.title: Passing Arguments to a Thread
docs.text:
You can pass a single value to a thread by casting a pointer to void*.

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>

void* printMessage(void* msg) {
    // Cast the void* argument back to its original type
    char* message = (char*) msg;
    std::cout << message << std::endl;
    return nullptr;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t thread1, thread2;
    const char* message1 = "This is thread 1.";
    const char* message2 = "This is thread 2.";

    // Create threads and pass a string literal to each
    pthread_create(&thread1, nullptr, printMessage, (void*) message1);
    pthread_create(&thread2, nullptr, printMessage, (void*) message2);

    // Wait for the threads to finish
    pthread_join(thread1, nullptr);
    pthread_join(thread2, nullptr);

    return 0;
}

Sample Output:

This is thread 1.
This is thread 2.

docs.title: Passing Multiple Values
docs.text:
To pass multiple values, you must bundle them into a struct and pass a pointer to an instance of that struct.

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <string>

// A struct to hold multiple arguments for our thread
struct ThreadArgs {
    int id;
    std::string message;
};

void* printArgs(void* arg) {
    // Cast the void* back to our struct type
    ThreadArgs* args = (ThreadArgs*) arg;

    std::cout << "Thread ID: " << args->id
              << ", Message: '" << args->message << "'" << std::endl;

    // Free the dynamically allocated memory to avoid leaks
    delete args;

    return nullptr;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t thread1;

    // IMPORTANT: Allocate the struct on the heap, not the stack,
    // to ensure it still exists when the new thread accesses it.
    ThreadArgs* args = new ThreadArgs();
    args->id = 101;
    args->message = "Passing multiple values is easy!";

    // Create the thread, passing a pointer to the struct
    pthread_create(&thread1, nullptr, printArgs, (void*) args);
    pthread_join(thread1, nullptr);

    return 0;
}

Sample Output:

Thread ID: 101, Message: 'Passing multiple values is easy!'

docs.title: 2. The Power of Parallelism
docs.text: Now, let's explore why using multiple threads can significantly speed up our programs. We'll do this by writing a program to count prime numbers in a given range, first sequentially and then in parallel.

docs.title: Measuring Time Accurately: Monotonic Clocks
docs.text: To measure the performance of our sequential and parallel code, we need an accurate timer. For benchmarking, we should use a monotonic clock. A monotonic clock is a clock that can only move forward and is not affected by system time changes (like a user manually changing the time or daylight saving adjustments). This property ensures that the time duration we measure between two points is always positive and accurately reflects the elapsed time. In C++, std::chrono::steady_clock is guaranteed to be monotonic and is the best choice for measuring time intervals.

docs.title: The isPrime() Function
docs.text:
We need a function that does a fair amount of work to properly see the benefits of parallelism. Checking for prime numbers is a good example of a CPU-intensive task.

// A simple function to check if a number is prime
bool isPrime(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return false;
    for (int i = 2; i * i <= n; ++i) {
        if (n % i == 0) return false;
    }
    return true;
}

Algorithm Explanation:

This function checks if a number n is prime by trying to divide it by numbers starting from 2 up to the square root of n. If n is divisible by any number in this range, it cannot be a prime number. We only need to check up to the square root because if a number n has a divisor larger than its square root, it must also have a divisor smaller than it.

docs.title: The Full Program: Sequential vs. Parallel
docs.text:
The program below will first count primes sequentially and then do it in parallel, finally printing a comparison of the results.

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <chrono>
#include <vector>

#define NUM_THREADS 4 // Feel free to change this based on your CPU cores

// isPrime function is defined above

// Struct to pass data to our prime counting threads
struct PrimeCounterData {
    int start;
    int end;
    int count;
};

void* countPrimes(void* arg) {
    PrimeCounterData* data = (PrimeCounterData*) arg;
    data->count = 0;
    for (int i = data->start; i < data->end; ++i) {
        if (isPrime(i)) {
            data->count++;
        }
    }
    return nullptr;
}

int main() {
    const int N = 200000;

    // --- SEQUENTIAL EXECUTION ---
    std::cout << "--- Sequential Execution ---" << std::endl;
    auto start_time_seq = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    int sequential_prime_count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
        if (isPrime(i)) sequential_prime_count++;
    }
    auto end_time_seq = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    std::chrono::duration<double> sequential_time = end_time_seq - start_time_seq;
    std::cout << "Primes found: " << sequential_prime_count << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Time taken: " << sequential_time.count() << " seconds" << std::endl << std::endl;

    // --- PARALLEL EXECUTION ---
    std::cout << "--- Parallel Execution (" << NUM_THREADS << " threads) ---" << std::endl;
    auto start_time_parallel = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    pthread_t threads[NUM_THREADS];
    PrimeCounterData thread_data[NUM_THREADS];
    int total_primes_parallel = 0;
    int chunk_size = N / NUM_THREADS;

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; ++i) {
        thread_data[i].start = i * chunk_size;
        thread_data[i].end = (i == NUM_THREADS - 1) ? N : (i + 1) * chunk_size;
        pthread_create(&threads[i], nullptr, countPrimes, &thread_data[i]);
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; ++i) {
        pthread_join(threads[i], nullptr);
        total_primes_parallel += thread_data[i].count;
    }

    auto end_time_parallel = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    std::chrono::duration<double> parallel_time = end_time_parallel - start_time_parallel;
    std::cout << "Primes found: " << total_primes_parallel << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Time taken: " << parallel_time.count() << " seconds" << std::endl << std::endl;

    // --- ANALYSIS ---
    std::cout << "--- Analysis ---" << std::endl;
    double speedup = sequential_time.count() / parallel_time.count();
    double efficiency = speedup / NUM_THREADS;
    std::cout << "Speedup: " << speedup << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Efficiency: " << efficiency << std::endl;

    return 0;
}

Sample Output (will vary based on your machine):

--- Sequential Execution ---
Primes found: 17984
Time taken: 0.234567 seconds

--- Parallel Execution (4 threads) ---
Primes found: 17984
Time taken: 0.061234 seconds

--- Analysis ---
Speedup: 3.8309
Efficiency: 0.9577

docs.title: 3. Thread Synchronization
docs.text: When multiple threads access and modify shared data concurrently, it can lead to unpredictable results. This situation is known as a race condition. The section of code accessing the shared resource is called the critical section.

docs.title: Demonstrating a Race Condition
docs.text:
Let's look at a simple example where multiple threads increment a shared counter without any protection.

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>

#define NUM_THREADS 10
#define INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD 100000

long long shared_counter = 0;

void* incrementCounter(void* arg) {
    for (int i = 0; i < INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD; ++i) {
        shared_counter++; // RACE CONDITION HERE!
    }
    return nullptr;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t threads[NUM_THREADS];

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; ++i) {
        pthread_create(&threads[i], nullptr, incrementCounter, nullptr);
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; ++i) {
        pthread_join(threads[i], nullptr);
    }

    std::cout << "Expected counter value: " << (long long)NUM_THREADS * INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Actual counter value:   " << shared_counter << std::endl;

    return 0;
}

Sample Output (will likely vary with each run):

Expected counter value: 1000000
Actual counter value:   784321

What Went Wrong? The shared_counter++ operation is not atomic; it's a sequence of read-modify-write. A race condition occurs when one thread reads the counter's value, but before it can write the new value back, the scheduler switches to another thread. That thread also reads the same original value. Both threads write back an incremented value, but one of the updates is lost.

docs.title: Fixing the Race Condition with Mutexes
docs.text:
A mutex (mutual exclusion) is a synchronization primitive that acts like a lock. It can be used to protect a critical section, ensuring that only one thread can execute that code at a time.

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>

#define NUM_THREADS 10
#define INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD 100000

long long shared_counter = 0;
pthread_mutex_t mutex; // Declare the mutex

void* incrementCounter(void* arg) {
    for (int i = 0; i < INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD; ++i) {
        pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex);   // Lock the mutex
        shared_counter++;             // CRITICAL SECTION
        pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex); // Unlock the mutex
    }
    return nullptr;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t threads[NUM_THREADS];

    pthread_mutex_init(&mutex, nullptr); // Initialize the mutex

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; ++i) {
        pthread_create(&threads[i], nullptr, incrementCounter, nullptr);
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; ++i) {
        pthread_join(threads[i], nullptr);
    }

    pthread_mutex_destroy(&mutex); // Destroy the mutex

    std::cout << "Expected counter value: " << (long long)NUM_THREADS * INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Actual counter value:   " << shared_counter << std::endl;
    return 0;
}

Explanation: * pthread_mutex_init(&mutex, nullptr): Initializes the mutex before use. * pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex): A thread attempts to acquire the lock. If another thread holds it, this thread will wait (block). * pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex): The thread releases the lock, allowing another waiting thread to proceed. * pthread_mutex_destroy(&mutex): Frees any resources associated with the mutex when it is no longer needed.

Sample Output:

Expected counter value: 1000000
Actual counter value:   1000000

docs.title: Pthread Library Tutorial: Thread Creation and Synchronization
Introduction
docs.text: Welcome to this comprehensive tutorial on the Pthread (POSIX Threads) library in C++. In this lab, you'll learn the fundamentals of thread creation and understand why thread synchronization is crucial in multithreaded programming. By the end of this tutorial, you'll be able to create threads, pass data between them, and understand the challenges that arise when threads work together.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Basic knowledge of C++ programming
  • Understanding of functions and pointers
  • Familiarity with compilation using g++

docs.title: Compilation Instructions
docs.text:
Throughout this tutorial, compile your programs using: 

g++ -pthread -o program_name source_file.cpp

The -pthread flag links the pthread library to your program.

docs.title: 1.1 Basic Thread Creation
docs.text:
Let's start with the most fundamental concept: creating and managing threads.

Key Functions: - pthread_create(): Creates a new thread - pthread_join(): Waits for a thread to complete - pthread_exit(): Terminates the current thread

Basic Syntax: 

int pthread_create(pthread_t *thread, const pthread_attr_t *attr,
                   void *(*start_routine)(void *), void *arg);
int pthread_join(pthread_t thread, void **retval);

Let's create our first threaded program:

Example 1.1: Basic Thread Creation

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <unistd.h>

// Thread function - this is what the thread will execute
void* threadFunction(void* arg) {
    std::cout << "Hello from thread! Thread ID: " << pthread_self() << std::endl;

    // Simulate some work
    sleep(2);

    std::cout << "Thread finishing execution" << std::endl;
    return nullptr;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t thread;

    std::cout << "Main thread starting. Main thread ID: " << pthread_self() << std::endl;

    // Create the thread
    int result = pthread_create(&thread, nullptr, threadFunction, nullptr);

    if (result != 0) {
        std::cerr << "Error creating thread!" << std::endl;
        return 1;
    }

    std::cout << "Thread created successfully" << std::endl;

    // Wait for the thread to complete
    pthread_join(thread, nullptr);

    std::cout << "Main thread ending" << std::endl;
    return 0;
}

What's happening here?

  1. We define a thread function threadFunction() that takes a void* parameter and returns void*
  2. In main(), we declare a pthread_t variable to hold the thread identifier
  3. pthread_create() creates the thread with default attributes (nullptr)
  4. pthread_join() makes the main thread wait for the worker thread to finish
  5. Both threads have unique IDs that we can print using pthread_self()

Expected Output: 

Main thread starting. Main thread ID: [some number]
Thread created successfully
Hello from thread! Thread ID: [different number]
Thread finishing execution
Main thread ending

docs.title: 1.2 Thread with Parameters
docs.text:
Now let's learn how to pass data to threads. Since pthread_create() accepts only a void* parameter, we need to use structures to pass multiple values.

Example 1.2: Passing Data to Threads

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <string>

// Structure to hold thread parameters
struct ThreadData {
    int id;
    std::string message;
    int count;
};

// Thread function that uses the passed data
void* threadFunction(void* arg) {
    // Cast the void* back to our structure
    ThreadData* data = static_cast<ThreadData*>(arg);

    std::cout << "Thread " << data->id << " started" << std::endl;

    // Use the data passed to the thread
    for (int i = 0; i < data->count; i++) {
        std::cout << "Thread " << data->id << ": " << data->message 
                  << " (iteration " << (i + 1) << ")" << std::endl;
    }

    std::cout << "Thread " << data->id << " finished" << std::endl;
    return nullptr;
}

int main() {
    const int NUM_THREADS = 3;
    pthread_t threads[NUM_THREADS];
    ThreadData threadData[NUM_THREADS];

    std::cout << "Creating " << NUM_THREADS << " threads..." << std::endl;

    // Create multiple threads with different data
    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; i++) {
        threadData[i].id = i + 1;
        threadData[i].message = "Hello from thread " + std::to_string(i + 1);
        threadData[i].count = (i + 1) * 2;  // Different work load for each thread

        int result = pthread_create(&threads[i], nullptr, threadFunction, &threadData[i]);

        if (result != 0) {
            std::cerr << "Error creating thread " << i << std::endl;
            return 1;
        }
    }

    // Wait for all threads to complete
    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; i++) {
        pthread_join(threads[i], nullptr);
    }

    std::cout << "All threads completed!" << std::endl;
    return 0;
}

Key Points: - We use a struct to package multiple parameters - Each thread gets its own copy of the data structure - We cast void* back to our structure type inside the thread function - Multiple threads can run concurrently, so output order may vary

docs.title: 2.1 Understanding the isPrime() Algorithm
docs.text:
Before we dive into parallel programming, let's understand our example algorithm. We'll use prime number checking because it's computationally intensive and naturally parallelizable.

Prime Number Checking Algorithm:

bool isPrime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) return false;
    if (n == 2) return true;
    if (n % 2 == 0) return false;

    // Check odd divisors up to sqrt(n)
    for (int i = 3; i * i <= n; i += 2) {
        if (n % i == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

Why is this good for parallelism? 1. Independent computations: Checking if number X is prime doesn't depend on checking number Y 2. CPU-intensive: Lots of mathematical operations that can benefit from parallel processing 3. Scalable workload: We can easily divide the range of numbers among multiple threads

docs.title: 2.2 Simple Sequential Example
docs.text:
Let's establish our baseline with a sequential (single-threaded) implementation:

Example 2.2: Sequential Prime Counting

#include <iostream>
#include <chrono>

bool isPrime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) return false;
    if (n == 2) return true;
    if (n % 2 == 0) return false;

    for (int i = 3; i * i <= n; i += 2) {
        if (n % i == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int countPrimesSequential(int start, int end) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = start; i <= end; i++) {
        if (isPrime(i)) {
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

int main() {
    const int START = 1;
    const int END = 100000;

    std::cout << "Counting primes from " << START << " to " << END << " (sequential)" << std::endl;

    // Measure execution time
    auto start_time = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();

    int primeCount = countPrimesSequential(START, END);

    auto end_time = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    auto duration = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>(end_time - start_time);

    std::cout << "Found " << primeCount << " prime numbers" << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Sequential execution time: " << duration.count() << " milliseconds" << std::endl;

    return 0;
}

Run this program and note the execution time. This will be our baseline for comparison.

docs.title: 2.3 Parallelism Example
docs.text: Now let's harness the power of multiple threads to speed up our computation!

docs.title: 2.3.1 countPrimesSequential() Analysis
docs.text: Our sequential function processes numbers one by one in a single thread: - Input: Range of numbers (start to end) - Process: Check each number individually - Output: Count of prime numbers - Limitation: Uses only one CPU core

docs.title: 2.3.2 countPrimesParallel() Components
docs.text:
To parallelize this, we need three key components:

Component 1: Thread Data Structure 

struct ThreadData {
    int start;        // Starting number for this thread
    int end;          // Ending number for this thread
    int result;       // Store the count of primes found
    int threadId;     // For identification and debugging
};

Component 2: Thread Function 

void* countPrimesThread(void* arg) {
    ThreadData* data = static_cast<ThreadData*>(arg);

    std::cout << "Thread " << data->threadId 
              << " processing range [" << data->start 
              << ", " << data->end << "]" << std::endl;

    data->result = 0;
    for (int i = data->start; i <= data->end; i++) {
        if (isPrime(i)) {
            data->result++;
        }
    }

    std::cout << "Thread " << data->threadId 
              << " found " << data->result << " primes" << std::endl;

    return nullptr;
}

Component 3: Work Distribution Strategy 

// Divide the work evenly among threads
int rangeSize = (END - START + 1) / NUM_THREADS;
for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; i++) {
    threadData[i].start = START + i * rangeSize;
    threadData[i].end = (i == NUM_THREADS - 1) ? END : threadData[i].start + rangeSize - 1;
    threadData[i].threadId = i;
}

docs.title: 2.3.3 Complete Parallel Program
docs.text:
Example 2.3: Parallel Prime Counting

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <chrono>

struct ThreadData {
    int start;
    int end;
    int result;
    int threadId;
};

bool isPrime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) return false;
    if (n == 2) return true;
    if (n % 2 == 0) return false;

    for (int i = 3; i * i <= n; i += 2) {
        if (n % i == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

void* countPrimesThread(void* arg) {
    ThreadData* data = static_cast<ThreadData*>(arg);

    std::cout << "Thread " << data->threadId 
              << " processing range [" << data->start 
              << ", " << data->end << "]" << std::endl;

    data->result = 0;
    for (int i = data->start; i <= data->end; i++) {
        if (isPrime(i)) {
            data->result++;
        }
    }

    std::cout << "Thread " << data->threadId 
              << " found " << data->result << " primes" << std::endl;

    return nullptr;
}

int countPrimesParallel(int start, int end, int numThreads) {
    pthread_t* threads = new pthread_t[numThreads];
    ThreadData* threadData = new ThreadData[numThreads];

    // Distribute work among threads
    int rangeSize = (end - start + 1) / numThreads;

    std::cout << "Creating " << numThreads << " threads for parallel processing..." << std::endl;

    // Create threads
    for (int i = 0; i < numThreads; i++) {
        threadData[i].start = start + i * rangeSize;
        threadData[i].end = (i == numThreads - 1) ? end : threadData[i].start + rangeSize - 1;
        threadData[i].threadId = i;
        threadData[i].result = 0;

        int result = pthread_create(&threads[i], nullptr, countPrimesThread, &threadData[i]);
        if (result != 0) {
            std::cerr << "Error creating thread " << i << std::endl;
            return -1;
        }
    }

    // Wait for all threads to complete
    for (int i = 0; i < numThreads; i++) {
        pthread_join(threads[i], nullptr);
    }

    // Combine results from all threads
    int totalPrimes = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < numThreads; i++) {
        totalPrimes += threadData[i].result;
    }

    delete[] threads;
    delete[] threadData;

    return totalPrimes;
}

// Sequential version for comparison
int countPrimesSequential(int start, int end) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = start; i <= end; i++) {
        if (isPrime(i)) {
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

int main() {
    const int START = 1;
    const int END = 100000;
    const int NUM_THREADS = 4;

    std::cout << "=== Prime Number Counting Performance Comparison ===" << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Range: " << START << " to " << END << std::endl << std::endl;

    // Sequential execution
    std::cout << "1. Sequential Execution:" << std::endl;
    auto start_time = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    int sequentialResult = countPrimesSequential(START, END);
    auto end_time = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    auto sequentialDuration = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>(end_time - start_time);

    std::cout << "Found " << sequentialResult << " prime numbers" << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Sequential time: " << sequentialDuration.count() << " ms" << std::endl << std::endl;

    // Parallel execution
    std::cout << "2. Parallel Execution (" << NUM_THREADS << " threads):" << std::endl;
    start_time = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    int parallelResult = countPrimesParallel(START, END, NUM_THREADS);
    end_time = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    auto parallelDuration = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>(end_time - start_time);

    std::cout << "Found " << parallelResult << " prime numbers" << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Parallel time: " << parallelDuration.count() << " ms" << std::endl << std::endl;

    // Performance analysis
    std::cout << "=== Performance Analysis ===" << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Correctness check: " << (sequentialResult == parallelResult ? "PASSED" : "FAILED") << std::endl;

    if (parallelDuration.count() > 0) {
        double speedup = static_cast<double>(sequentialDuration.count()) / parallelDuration.count();
        std::cout << "Speedup: " << speedup << "x" << std::endl;
        std::cout << "Efficiency: " << (speedup / NUM_THREADS) * 100 << "%" << std::endl;
    }

    return 0;
}

Expected Output Analysis:

When you run this program, you should see: 1. Correctness: Both methods should find the same number of primes 2. Performance: The parallel version should be faster (speedup depends on your CPU) 3. Thread Activity: You'll see each thread reporting its assigned range and results

Try experimenting with different values: - Change NUM_THREADS (try 2, 4, 8) - Change the range (try 1 to 50000 or 1 to 200000) - Observe how performance changes

docs.title: Conceptual Foundation
docs.text:
So far, our threads have worked independently—each thread processed its own range of numbers without interacting with others. This worked well because: - Each thread had its own data - No thread needed to access shared resources - Results were combined only after all threads finished

However, in many real-world scenarios, threads need to: - Share data structures (arrays, lists, counters) - Access shared resources (files, network connections) - Coordinate their activities

docs.title: Critical Section Concept
docs.text:
A critical section is a code segment where threads access shared resources. Problems arise when multiple threads enter the critical section simultaneously.

Example of a Critical Section: 

// Shared variable
int globalCounter = 0;

// Critical section - accessing shared variable
void incrementCounter() {
    globalCounter++;  // This is NOT atomic!
}

The increment operation globalCounter++ actually involves three steps: 1. Read the current value of globalCounter 2. Add 1 to that value 3. Write the new value back to globalCounter

If two threads execute these steps simultaneously, we can lose updates!

docs.title: Overview of Synchronization Mechanisms
docs.text:
Mutex (Mutual Exclusion): - Ensures only one thread can access a critical section at a time - Like a lock on a bathroom door

Semaphore: - Controls access to a resource with limited capacity - Like a parking lot with limited spaces

Condition Variables: - Allow threads to wait for certain conditions - Like waiting for a signal to proceed

In this tutorial, we'll focus on mutex as it's the most fundamental synchronization mechanism.

docs.title: Part 4: The Problem - Race Conditions
docs.text: Let's demonstrate why synchronization is necessary by creating a program that exhibits race conditions.

docs.title: Race Condition Demonstration
docs.text:
Example 4.1: The Broken Counter

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>

// Shared global variable - THIS IS THE PROBLEM!
int globalCounter = 0;
const int INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD = 100000;

struct ThreadData {
    int threadId;
};

void* incrementCounter(void* arg) {
    ThreadData* data = static_cast<ThreadData*>(arg);

    std::cout << "Thread " << data->threadId << " starting to increment..." << std::endl;

    // Each thread increments the counter many times
    for (int i = 0; i < INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD; i++) {
        globalCounter++;  // RACE CONDITION: Multiple threads accessing globalCounter
    }

    std::cout << "Thread " << data->threadId << " finished incrementing" << std::endl;
    return nullptr;
}

int main() {
    const int NUM_THREADS = 4;
    pthread_t threads[NUM_THREADS];
    ThreadData threadData[NUM_THREADS];

    std::cout << "=== Race Condition Demonstration ===" << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Expected final value: " << (NUM_THREADS * INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD) << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Initial counter value: " << globalCounter << std::endl << std::endl;

    // Create threads
    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; i++) {
        threadData[i].threadId = i;
        pthread_create(&threads[i], nullptr, incrementCounter, &threadData[i]);
    }

    // Wait for all threads to complete
    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; i++) {
        pthread_join(threads[i], nullptr);
    }

    std::cout << std::endl << "=== Results ===" << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Final counter value: " << globalCounter << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Expected value: " << (NUM_THREADS * INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD) << std::endl;

    if (globalCounter == (NUM_THREADS * INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD)) {
        std::cout << "Result: CORRECT (lucky!)" << std::endl;
    } else {
        std::cout << "Result: INCORRECT - Race condition occurred!" << std::endl;
        std::cout << "Lost updates: " << (NUM_THREADS * INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD) - globalCounter << std::endl;
    }

    return 0;
}

docs.title: Analysis: What Goes Wrong and Why
docs.text:
Run this program multiple times. You'll likely see different results each time, and the final counter value will often be less than expected.

Why does this happen?

  1. The increment operation globalCounter++ is not atomic: 

    Thread A: Read globalCounter (value = 100)
Thread B: Read globalCounter (value = 100)  ← Same value!
Thread A: Calculate 100 + 1 = 101
Thread B: Calculate 100 + 1 = 101          ← Same calculation!
Thread A: Write 101 to globalCounter
Thread B: Write 101 to globalCounter       ← Overwrites A's work!

  2. Lost updates: When two threads read the same value and both increment it, one increment is lost.

  3. Non-deterministic behavior: The timing of thread execution is unpredictable, leading to different results each run.

Try running the program with different parameters: - Reduce INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD to 1000 - does the problem still occur? - Increase NUM_THREADS to 8 - does the problem get worse? - Add sleep() calls in the loop - how does this affect the race condition?

docs.title: Understanding the Race Window
docs.text:
The "race window" is the time between reading a shared variable and writing back to it. The longer this window, the more likely race conditions become.

// Wider race window
int temp = globalCounter;  // Step 1: Read
temp = temp + 1;          // Step 2: Modify  
globalCounter = temp;     // Step 3: Write
// More time for another thread to interfere!

// Narrower race window
globalCounter++;          // All three steps together
// Still not atomic, but smaller window

docs.title: Summary: Why We Need Synchronization
docs.text:
This demonstration shows that even simple operations like incrementing a counter can go wrong in multithreaded environments. We need synchronization mechanisms to:

  1. Ensure atomicity: Operations on shared data complete without interference
  2. Prevent race conditions: Control access to critical sections
  3. Maintain data consistency: Ensure shared data remains in a valid state
  4. Provide predictable behavior: Make multithreaded programs deterministic

In the next part of this tutorial series, we'll learn how to fix these problems using mutex locks and other synchronization techniques.
